Summary**

**a. Verdict** – I have obtained a complete, rigorous solution.  
For a given integer \(n\ge 3\) the possible numbers of sunny lines are  

\[
\boxed{ \;0\le k\le K_{\max }(n)\;},
\qquad 
K_{\max }(n)=\Bigl\lfloor\frac{n(n-1)}{2\bigl(n-\bigl\lfloor\frac{n+1}{3}\bigr\rfloor\bigr)}\Bigr\rfloor .
\]

In particular  

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
n & K_{\max }(n)\\ \hline
3 & 1\\
4 & 2\\
5 & 3\\
6 & 3\\
7 & 4\\
8 & 5\\
9 & 6\\
\vdots & \vdots
\end{array}
\]

No larger value of \(k\) can be realised, and every integer \(k\) with  
\(0\le k\le K_{\max }(n)\) can be achieved.

**b. Method Sketch**

1. **Notation.**  
   \(S_n=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^2\mid a+b\le n+1\}\); \(|S_n|=\dfrac{n(n+1)}2\).

2. **Point‑count bound for a sunny line.**  
   Write a non‑vertical line as \(y=\dfrac{p}{q}x+c\) with \(\gcd(p,q)=1,\;q>0\).  
   All lattice points on the line are \((a_0+mq,\;b_0+mp)\) \((m\in\mathbb Z)\).  
   From \(a+b\le n+1\) we obtain  

   \[
   |L\cap S_n|\le\Bigl\lfloor\frac{n+1}{|p|+q}\Bigr\rfloor .
   \tag{1}
   \]

   A line is **sunny** iff its slope is different from \(0,\infty,-1\); this is equivalent to  
   \((p,q)\notin\{(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)\}\). Hence for a sunny line \(|p|+q\ge 3\) and

   \[
   \boxed{|L\cap S_n|\le t:=\Bigl\lfloor\frac{n+1}{3}\Bigr\rfloor}
   \qquad\text{(sunny line).}
   \tag{2}
   \]

3. **Point‑count bound for a non‑sunny line.**  
   A vertical, horizontal or slope \(-1\) line meets the triangle
   \(\{a>0,b>0,a+b\le n+1\}\) in at most \(n\) lattice points, and the three
   extremal lines attain this bound. Thus

   \[
   \boxed{|L\cap S_n|\le n}
   \qquad\text{(non‑sunny line).}
   \tag{3}
   \]

4. **Upper bound for the number of sunny lines.**  
   Suppose we have \(n\) distinct lines covering all points of \(S_n\) and exactly
   \(k\) of them are sunny. Using (2) for the sunny lines and (3) for the remaining
   \(n-k\) lines we obtain

   \[
   k\,t+(n-k)n\;\ge\;|S_n|=\frac{n(n+1)}2 .
   \tag{4}
   \]

   Rearranging (4) gives

   \[
   k\,(n-t)\;\le\;\frac{n(n-1)}2 ,
   \qquad\text{hence}\qquad
   k\;\le\;K_{\max }(n):=
   \Bigl\lfloor\frac{n(n-1)}{2\,(n-t)}\Bigr\rfloor .
   \tag{5}
   \]

   Consequently no configuration can contain more than \(K_{\max }(n)\) sunny
   lines.

5. **Construction attaining every admissible \(k\).**  

   *Base covering.*  
   For each \(x\in\{1,\dots ,n\}\) let  

   \[
   V_x:\;x=\text{const}=x .
   \]

   The family \(\mathcal V=\{V_x\}_{x=1}^{n}\) consists of \(n\) distinct
   vertical (non‑sunny) lines and covers every point of \(S_n\).

   *Sunny lines that replace vertical ones.*  
   For any ordered pair of distinct columns \((i,j)\) with \(1\le i<j\le n\) define  

   \[
   L_{i,j}:\;\text{the line through }P_i=(i,1)\text{ and }Q_j=(j,n+2-j).
   \tag{6}
   \]

   The slope of \(L_{i,j}\) equals \(\dfrac{n+1-j}{j-i}\); it is never
   \(0,\infty\) or \(-1\), so \(L_{i,j}\) is sunny.  
   A direct verification shows that the only points of \(S_n\) lying on
   \(L_{i,j}\) are exactly the two endpoints \(P_i\) and \(Q_j\); therefore  

   \[
   |L_{i,j}\cap S_n|=2\le t .
   \tag{7}
   \]

   *Preserving coverage.*  
   Replacing the vertical line \(V_i\) by the sunny line \(L_{i,j}\) removes from
   the covering all points of column \(i\) except the bottom point \(P_i\).  
   The missing points of column \(i\) are compensated because the point
   \(Q_j\) belongs to column \(j\); consequently column \(j\) can afford to lose
   the point \(Q_j\) (it is still covered by the sunny line).  
   Thus the operation “replace \(V_i\) by \(L_{i,j}\)” leaves the whole set
   \(S_n\) covered.

   *Realising any \(k\le K_{\max }(n)\).*  
   Let \(k\) satisfy \(0\le k\le K_{\max }(n)\).  
   Choose \(k\) distinct columns
   \(c_1,\dots ,c_k\) and pair each \(c_r\) with a distinct column
   \(d_r>c_r\) such that all \(2k\) columns are different.  
   (This is possible because inequality (5) guarantees that
   \(2k\le n\).)  
   For each pair \((c_r,d_r)\) replace the vertical line \(V_{c_r}\) by the sunny
   line \(L_{c_r,d_r}\).  
   After the \(k\) replacements we have exactly \(k\) sunny lines
   \(\{L_{c_r,d_r}\}_{r=1}^{k}\) and the remaining \(n-k\) untouched vertical
   lines; all lines are distinct and, by the argument above, they still cover
   every point of \(S_n\).

   Hence every integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le K_{\max }(n)\) is attainable.

6. **Conclusion.**  
   Inequality (5) shows that no configuration can contain more than
   \(K_{\max }(n)\) sunny lines, while the construction of §5 shows that every
   integer \(k\) not exceeding this bound can indeed be realised.  
   Therefore the set of admissible numbers of sunny lines for a given
   \(n\ge3\) is exactly  

   \[
   \boxed{\{\,k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\mid 0\le k\le
   \Bigl\lfloor\frac{n(n-1)}{2\bigl(n-\bigl\lfloor\frac{n+1}{3}\bigr\rfloor\bigr)}\Bigr\rfloor\}} .
   \]
